title: Model without recurrence requires explicit positional encodings
description: Since the Transformer contains no recurrence and no convolution, it must inject information about the relative or absolute position of tokens via positional encodings added to the input embeddings.
canonical_description: model without recurrence requires explicit positional encodings

evidence.anchor: Since our model contains no recurrence and no convolution, in order for the model to make use of the order of the sequence
evidence.quote: Since our model contains no recurrence and no convolution, in order for the model to make use of the order of the sequence, we must inject some information about the relative or absolute position of the tokens in the sequence.

verdict.reasoning: The gap's claim is that non-recurrent models require explicit positional encodings added to input embeddings. Three papers (Dynamic Position Encoding, Alternative positional encoding functions, Speech RPE) do not address the gap at all — they take the necessity as given and simply improve the encoding method. Paper 1 (Relative Position Representations) modifies the attention mechanism to carry relative position signals instead of adding encodings to input embeddings, but still requires explicit learned position representations (w^K, w^V vectors). It challenges the "added to input embeddings" wording but does not refute the need for explicit position information in non-recurrent models. Paper 5 (PRformer) eliminates explicit positional encodings by adding recurrence (RNN/GRU layers), which actually reinforces the gap's premise — add recurrence, and you no longer need positional encodings. It does not show a purely feedforward/attention-only model working without explicit position information. Thus, the fundamental claim that non-recurrent Transformers require explicit position information remains unaddressed by the subsequent literature.

paper.title: Self-Attention with Relative Position Representations
paper.abstract: Relying entirely on an attention mechanism, the Transformer introduced by Vaswani et al. (2017) achieves state-of-the-art results for machine translation. In contrast to recurrent and convolutional neural networks, it does not explicitly model relative or absolute position information in its structure. Instead, it requires adding representations of absolute positions to its inputs. In this work we present an alternative approach, extending the self-attention mechanism to efficiently consider representations of the relative positions, or distances between sequence elements. On the WMT 2014 English-to-German and English-to-French translation tasks, this approach yields improvements of 1.3 BLEU and 0.3 BLEU over absolute position representations, respectively. Notably, we observe that combining relative and absolute position representations yields no further improvement in translation quality. We describe an efficient implementation of our method and cast it as an instance of relation-aware self-attention mechanisms that can generalize to arbitrary graph-labeled inputs.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper proposes relative position representations that are incorporated directly into the self-attention mechanism of the Transformer, rather than being added to input embeddings as absolute positional encodings. The approach modifies the attention compatibility function and output computation to use learned representations of relative distances between sequence elements, with clipping beyond a maximum distance k. On WMT translation tasks, this method matches or outperforms the standard sinusoidal absolute position encodings, and combining both yields no further improvement.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap states that non-recurrent models "must inject information about the relative or absolute position of tokens via positional encodings added to the input embeddings." This paper shows that positional information can instead be injected through modifications to the attention mechanism itself, without adding anything to input embeddings. However, the paper does not eliminate the need for explicit position information altogether — it still requires learned relative position representations (w^K and w^V vectors) that are explicitly computed from position differences. The gap's specific claim about the necessity of adding positional encodings to input embeddings is challenged but not fully refuted, as the paper still relies on explicit position representations, just in a different form.
evidence_snippets: In this work we present an alternative approach, extending the self-attention mechanism to efficiently consider representations of the relative positions, or distances between sequence elements.
Even when entirely replacing its absolute position encodings, we demonstrate significant improvements in translation quality on two machine translation tasks.
In our experiments we did not observe any benefit from including sinusoidal position encodings in addition to relative position representations.

paper.title: Dynamic Position Encoding for Transformers
paper.abstract: Recurrent models have been dominating the field of neural machine translation (NMT) for the past few years. Transformers \citep{vaswani2017attention}, have radically changed it by proposing a novel architecture that relies on a feed-forward backbone and self-attention mechanism. Although Transformers are powerful, they could fail to properly encode sequential/positional information due to their non-recurrent nature. To solve this problem, position embeddings are defined exclusively for each time step to enrich word information. However, such embeddings are fixed after training regardless of the task and the word ordering system of the source or target language. In this paper, we propose a novel architecture with new position embeddings depending on the input text to address this shortcoming by taking the order of target words into consideration. Instead of using predefined position embeddings, our solution generates new embeddings to refine each word's position information. Since we do not dictate the position of source tokens and learn them in an end-to-end fashion, we refer to our method as dynamic position encoding (DPE). We evaluated the impact of our model on multiple datasets to translate from English into German, French, and Italian and observed meaningful improvements in comparison to the original Transformer.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes Dynamic Position Encoding (DPE), a method that generates position embeddings informed by target-side word order information, rather than using fixed sinusoidal position encodings. It adds a small neural network (two Transformer layers) between the input embeddings and the first encoder layer, trained with an auxiliary loss that encourages the generated embeddings to mimic position encodings of target-aligned positions. The paper shows modest BLEU improvements on several translation tasks.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not address the research gap at all. The gap states that non-recurrent models (like Transformers) require explicit positional encodings. The paper explicitly acknowledges this as a given fact ("they require an explicit summation of the input embeddings with position encoding") and builds on top of it by proposing a better way to compute those positional encodings. The fundamental question of whether explicit positional encodings are necessary for non-recurrent models remains completely open — the paper does not attempt to remove positional encodings, replace the Transformer's non-recurrent architecture, or demonstrate that positional information can be injected implicitly through other means.
evidence_snippets: Since Transformers have a non-recurrent architecture, they could face problems when encoding sequential data. As a result, they require an explicit summation of the input embeddings with position encoding to provide information about the order of each word.
The input to DPE is a source word embedding ($w_i$) summed with sinusoidal position ($p_i$) encoding ($w_i \oplus p_i$).

In the original Transformer, the position of $w_i$ is dictated by adding $p_i$, but the original position of this word is not always the best one for translation; thus $r_i$ is defined to address this problem.

paper.title: Alternative positional encoding functions for neural transformers
paper.abstract: A key module in neural transformer-based deep architectures is positional encoding. This module enables a suitable way to encode positional information as input for transformer neural layers. This success has been rooted in the use of sinusoidal functions of various frequencies, in order to capture recurrent patterns of differing typical periods. In this work, an alternative set of periodic functions is proposed for positional encoding. These functions preserve some key properties of sinusoidal ones, while they depart from them in fundamental ways. Some tentative experiments are reported, where the original sinusoidal version is substantially outperformed. This strongly suggests that the alternative functions may have a wider use in other transformer architectures.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes alternative periodic functions (triangular, square wave, sawtooth) to replace the standard sinusoidal functions used in Transformer positional encodings. It tests these on a machine translation task (Multi30K English-German) and reports that the alternatives outperform the sinusoidal baseline. However, the paper does not address the fundamental question of whether explicit positional encodings are necessary — it takes that requirement as given and works within that paradigm.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not address the gap at all. The gap states that models without recurrence (like Transformers) require explicit positional encodings. This paper does not challenge, solve, or even discuss this requirement — it simply proposes better functions for the positional encodings that are already known to be needed. The fundamental question of whether explicit positional encodings can be avoided or whether the requirement can be circumvented remains entirely open.
evidence_snippets: Transformer architectures rely on positional encodings to inject order information into sequences processed by permutation-invariant self-attention layers
The original Transformer uses a deterministic periodic encoding that assigns to each position m a vector PE(m)
Now, we propose to employ non sinusoidal functions for φ and ψ.

paper.title: Improving Generalization of Transformer for Speech Recognition with Parallel Schedule Sampling and Relative Positional Embedding
paper.abstract: Transformer has shown promising results in many sequence to sequence transformation tasks recently. It utilizes a number of feed-forward self-attention layers to replace the recurrent neural networks (RNN) in attention-based encoder decoder (AED) architecture. Self-attention layer learns temporal dependence by incorporating sinusoidal positional embedding of tokens in a sequence for parallel computing. Quicker iteration speed in training than sequential operation of RNN can be obtained. Deeper layers of the transformer also make it perform better than RNN-based AED. However, this parallelization ability is lost when applying scheduled sampling training. Self-attention with sinusoidal positional embedding may cause performance degradations for longer sequences that have similar acoustic or semantic information at different positions as well. To address these problems, we propose to use parallel scheduled sampling (PSS) and relative positional embedding (RPE) to help the transformer generalize to unseen data. Our proposed methods achieve a 7% relative improvement for short utterances and a 70% relative gain for long utterances on a 10,000-hour Mandarin ASR task.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes replacing absolute positional embeddings (APE) with relative positional embeddings (RPE) in Transformer-based speech recognition to improve generalization on long utterances. It also proposes parallel scheduled sampling (PSS) for training efficiency. The paper takes the necessity of explicit positional encodings as a given starting point and focuses on improving which type of encoding works better for speech tasks.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not address the fundamental gap that models without recurrence require explicit positional encodings. It fully accepts this premise — the baseline Transformer uses absolute positional embeddings, and the proposed RPE is still an explicit positional encoding added to the model. The gap about whether non-recurrent models can operate without any explicit positional encoding remains completely unaddressed.
evidence_snippets: Transformer contains no recurrence and convolution. In order to make use of the order of the sequence, input representations are added with absolute positional encoding before feeding to the encoder and decoder stacks.

The original APE proposed for NMT may not be suitable for speech recognition applications... Thus we want to use relative positional embedding for vanilla speech transformer to try to explore how the positional embedding affects long sentence recognition performance.

We first investigate APE in encoder. In $E5$, we remove APE in encoder and keep APE in decoder. Although SU drops a lot, LU even improves, which indicates APE can not generalize well on long sentences.

paper.title: PRformer: Pyramidal Recurrent Transformer for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
paper.abstract: The self-attention mechanism in Transformer architecture, invariant to sequence order, necessitates positional embeddings to encode temporal order in time series prediction. We argue that this reliance on positional embeddings restricts the Transformer's ability to effectively represent temporal sequences, particularly when employing longer lookback windows. To address this, we introduce an innovative approach that combines Pyramid RNN embeddings(PRE) for univariate time series with the Transformer's capability to model multivariate dependencies. PRE, utilizing pyramidal one-dimensional convolutional layers, constructs multiscale convolutional features that preserve temporal order. Additionally, RNNs, layered atop these features, learn multiscale time series representations sensitive to sequence order. This integration into Transformer models with attention mechanisms results in significant performance enhancements. We present the PRformer, a model integrating PRE with a standard Transformer encoder, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance on various real-world datasets. This performance highlights the effectiveness of our approach in leveraging longer lookback windows and underscores the critical role of robust temporal representations in maximizing Transformer's potential for prediction tasks. Code is available at this repository: \url{https://github.com/usualheart/PRformer}.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes PRformer, which replaces the standard positional encoding in Transformers with a Pyramid RNN Embedding (PRE) module for multivariate time series forecasting. PRE uses pyramidal convolutional layers followed by RNNs (GRU) to learn multi-scale temporal representations that inherently capture sequence order, thereby eliminating the need for explicit positional encodings. The paper demonstrates that this approach improves performance over standard Transformers with positional encodings on time series forecasting benchmarks.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper only addresses the gap for the specific domain of time series forecasting. It does not provide a general solution for removing positional encodings from Transformers across all domains (e.g., NLP, vision). Furthermore, the solution works by adding recurrence (RNN) to the architecture, which is consistent with the gap's premise — models without recurrence need positional encodings. The paper does not propose a way to make a purely feedforward/attention-based model (without recurrence) operate without positional encodings; instead it sidesteps the gap by injecting recurrence. The general theoretical question of whether a non-recurrent Transformer can inherently capture position without explicit encodings remains open.
evidence_snippets: As PRE embedding already captures the sequential relationships of the sequence, additional positional embeddings are unnecessary for representing the entire sequence of a univariate variable.

We propose using a Pyramidal RNN Embedding (PRE) module to replace the positional encoding in Transformers, addressing the deficiencies of Transformers in encoding sequential positional information relationships.

We employ PRE to learn representations of univariate time series, which serve as input to the Transformer model. This approach effectively addresses the deficiencies of Transformers in capturing positional information relationships within sequences.

ranking.feasibility_reasoning: Poses a fundamental architectural challenge: attention is permutation-equivariant by design — without position information, a Transformer literally cannot distinguish token order (bag-of-tokens behavior). The gap requires either (a) breaking permutation invariance in the attention mechanism without adding explicit position representations, or (b) encoding position implicitly through some other means (e.g., learned token identity hashing, input-dependent position signals). Neither approach has a clear, existing methodological handle. Published attempts either still use explicit position representations (Relative Position Representations uses w^K, w^V vectors) or add recurrence (PRformer) — exactly the workaround the gap excludes. Data and compute are not the bottleneck (standard benchmarks, moderate-scale models suffice), and the problem is well-scoped and evaluable (measure perplexity/accuracy without positional encodings). However, the core difficulty is mathematical rather than engineering: it demands a fundamental innovation to the attention operation itself, not an extension of known methods. This makes it low-tractability for a small team.
